title: Reading the Gospels
summary: What kind of books the Gospels are, who wrote them and when, the four distinct portraits of one Jesus, the Synoptic problem and the main solutions with their defenders, how John differs, and how to read the Gospels both side by side and one at a time.

sections.body:
The New Testament opens with four accounts of the life, teaching, death, and resurrection of Jesus, known by the names of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. The word gospel translates the Greek euangelion, ‘good news’, a word used in the Roman world for the announcement of a victory or the birth of an heir to the emperor. Mark's opening uses it for the whole story that follows: “This is the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” (Mark 1:1). (The last words, ‘the Son of God’, are missing from a few important early manuscripts, including the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus, and scholars debate whether they are original.) Only later did ‘gospel’ come to mean a kind of book.

The church could have kept one Gospel, or blended the four into one. In the second century some tried both. Marcion kept only an edited form of Luke. About AD 170 the Syrian Christian Tatian wove all four into a single narrative known as the Diatessaron (‘through four’), which was used in Syriac-speaking churches for centuries. But the church as a whole kept four separate books. Irenaeus of Lyons, writing about AD 180 (Against Heresies 3.11.8), argued that there could be neither more nor fewer than four, comparing them to the four winds and to the four living creatures around God's throne in Ezekiel and Revelation. From that comparison came the traditional symbols, fixed in the form most used today by Jerome: a man for Matthew, a lion for Mark, an ox for Luke, and an eagle for John.

Having four accounts is both a gift and a puzzle. It is a gift because each writer shows something the others do not, as four painters of the same face might. It is a puzzle because the four differ in order, wording, and emphasis, and the first three are so closely related that their relationship has been studied intensely for more than two centuries. This guide explains what the Gospels are, how they differ, and how scholars have explained their relationship.

sections.h: What kind of book is a Gospel?
sections.body:
In the early twentieth century, the scholars who founded form criticism, among them Karl Ludwig Schmidt, Martin Dibelius, and Rudolf Bultmann (whose History of the Synoptic Tradition appeared in 1921), argued that the Gospels were not biographies at all. They were folk literature, collections of units of oral tradition strung together by editors, a unique kind of writing with no real parallel. Martin Kähler had earlier described the Gospels as passion narratives with extended introductions, noting how much space they give to Jesus' last week.

That view has largely given way. Charles Talbert (What Is a Gospel?, 1977) and especially Richard Burridge (What Are the Gospels? A Comparison with Graeco-Roman Biography, 1992) compared the Gospels with ancient biographies, called bioi or ‘lives’: works such as Plutarch's Parallel Lives, Tacitus's Agricola, Suetonius's Lives of the Caesars, and Philostratus's Life of Apollonius of Tyana. They found that the Gospels share the genre's main features: a focus on one person, a narrative framed by his public career, a large share of space for his words and deeds, and attention to his death as revealing his character. Most scholars now accept that the Gospels are ancient biographies, of a distinctive Jewish and Christian kind. In the second century Justin Martyr already called them the ‘memoirs of the apostles’ (First Apology 66-67).

This matters for how they are read. Ancient biography was not modern biography. It did not aim at a complete chronology or a psychological portrait; it selected episodes and sayings that showed who a person was, and it often arranged material by topic rather than by date. Plutarch says as much at the start of his life of Alexander. So when Matthew gathers Jesus' teaching into five great discourses, or John places the clearing of the temple at the beginning of Jesus' ministry while the other three place it at the end, the reader should ask first what the arrangement is doing before assuming either writer is careless. Luke tells his reader directly that he has “carefully investigated everything from the beginning” in order to write “an orderly account” (Luke 1:3), and John says his book is selective and has a purpose: “these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31).

The Gospels are also more than biography. They are proclamation, written by believers for the life and faith of churches, and they present Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures. Richard Bauckham (The Gospels for All Christians, 1998) argued against the common assumption that each Gospel was written for a single isolated community, suggesting instead that they were written from the start to circulate among churches everywhere.

None of the four Gospels names its author in the text. The titles, ‘According to Matthew’, ‘According to Mark’, and so on, were attached early, and they appear uniformly in the manuscripts from the late second century onward; Martin Hengel (The Four Gospels and the One Gospel of Jesus Christ, 2000) argued that they must have been in use almost as soon as the books circulated together. The earliest external testimony comes from Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Asia Minor early in the second century, as quoted by the historian Eusebius (Church History 3.39). Papias reported, on the authority of an older figure he calls the elder, that Mark had been Peter's interpreter and wrote down accurately, though not in order, what he remembered of Peter's teaching about the Lord; and that Matthew arranged the sayings (the Greek word is logia) in the Hebrew language, and each translated them as he was able. What Papias meant by Matthew's ‘Hebrew’ sayings has been debated ever since, since our Gospel of Matthew does not read like a translation.

Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.1.1, about 180) gives the traditional picture: Matthew wrote for the Hebrews, Mark handed down Peter's preaching, Luke the companion of Paul recorded the gospel Paul preached, and John the disciple of the Lord published his Gospel while living at Ephesus. Many conservative scholars accept these attributions in substance. Many critical scholars regard them as later guesses and treat the Gospels as anonymous. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) argued that the Gospels are much closer to eyewitness testimony than form criticism assumed, and that the personal names in them often mark the eyewitnesses who were the sources of particular stories.

Dates depend partly on how the Gospels are related to each other and to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Jesus predicts in all three Synoptic Gospels (Mark 13:2 and parallels). Scholars who think the prediction reflects knowledge of the event date Matthew and Luke after 70; others note that the descriptions do not look like reports after the fact, and that Acts, Luke's second volume, ends with Paul still under house arrest in Rome about AD 62, which some take as evidence that Luke and Acts were finished before Paul's death. John A. T. Robinson (Redating the New Testament, 1976) argued that every New Testament book, John included, was written before 70; most scholars have not followed him that far.

sections.body:
Each Gospel has its own shape and its own way of presenting Jesus, and reading one straight through, rather than dipping into all four at random, is the best way to see it.

Matthew opens with a genealogy that presents Jesus as “the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1) and returns again and again to the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures, often with a formula such as ‘this took place to fulfill what the Lord had said through the prophet’. It gathers Jesus' teaching into five long discourses, each ending with a similar formula (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1): the Sermon on the Mount, the mission discourse, the parables, the discourse on the community, and the discourse on the end. Many readers see a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses and of Jesus as a new and greater Moses, who teaches from a mountain. Matthew is the only Gospel to use the word church (16:18; 18:17), and it ends with the risen Jesus sending his disciples to all nations.

Mark is the shortest and fastest, and probably the earliest. It has no birth story and begins with the adult Jesus. The Greek word euthys, ‘immediately’, runs through it dozens of times. Mark's Jesus is powerful and mysterious; he repeatedly commands silence about who he is, a feature William Wrede called the messianic secret in a 1901 book. The disciples misunderstand him again and again, and the question of the book is spoken by them in a boat: “Who is this, that even the wind and the sea obey Him?” (Mark 4:41). The answer is fully given only at the cross, where a Roman centurion says, “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39). The earliest manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8 with frightened women fleeing the empty tomb; the longer ending (16:9-20) is absent from Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and most scholars think it was added later. The guide on how we got the New Testament discusses this.

Luke is the first volume of a two-part work that continues in Acts, and it is the most self-consciously historical, beginning with a formal preface and dating events by the reigns of emperors and governors (Luke 2:1-2; 3:1-2). Luke gives unusual attention to outsiders: shepherds, Samaritans, tax collectors, sinners, the poor, and women, who appear far more often in Luke than in the others. It has many parables found nowhere else, including the Good Samaritan and the prodigal son. It stresses prayer, joy, and the Holy Spirit. Its long central section (9:51 to 19:27) is framed as Jesus' travel to Jerusalem, where the story and the salvation it announces are centered.

John differs most, and the next section describes how.

Matthew, Mark, and Luke are called the Synoptic Gospels, from a Greek word meaning ‘seen together’, because they can be set out in parallel columns and read side by side. A book that does this is called a synopsis; Kurt Aland's Synopsis of the Four Gospels is the standard one. Read this way, the three show an extraordinary degree of agreement, not only in the stories they tell but often in their order and their exact Greek wording. They also differ, in ways that are sometimes small and sometimes striking. Compare the rich man's question. In Mark and Luke Jesus replies, “Why do you call Me good?” (Mark 10:18; Luke 18:19). In Matthew the question and answer read, “Why do you ask Me about what is good?” (Matthew 19:17). The question of how three books came to be so alike and yet so different is called the Synoptic problem.

A few facts frame the problem. Nearly all of Mark's content appears in Matthew (about ninety percent of it) and a little over half in Luke. Material found in all three is called the triple tradition. Where the three share a story, Matthew and Luke seldom agree with each other in order against Mark: when one departs from Mark's order, the other usually keeps it. About two hundred and twenty to two hundred and thirty-five verses, mostly sayings of Jesus, such as the Lord's Prayer and much of the Sermon on the Mount, appear in Matthew and Luke but not in Mark; this is called the double tradition, and some of it is word for word, as in John the Baptist's “You brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Matthew 3:7; Luke 3:7). Each Gospel also has material of its own: Matthew's visit of the Magi, Luke's parable of the prodigal son. Such close verbal agreement, in Greek, across long passages, in reports of speech originally given in Aramaic, is very hard to explain unless some of the writers used the written work of others. Most scholars therefore think the problem is one of literary relationship, though a significant minority stresses oral tradition. The main solutions follow; each has been argued with great learning, and none commands complete agreement.

The Two-Source Hypothesis (also called the Two-Document Hypothesis) holds that Mark was written first, and that Matthew and Luke each used Mark and, independently, a second source, now lost, made up mostly of sayings. Scholars call it Q, from the German Quelle, ‘source’. The case for Mark's priority was developed in Germany in the nineteenth century: Karl Lachmann in 1835 noted the pattern of order, and Christian Hermann Weisse and Christian Gottlob Wilke in 1838 and Heinrich Julius Holtzmann in 1863 made the case at length. In English, B. H. Streeter's The Four Gospels (1924) gave it its classic form, adding special sources for Matthew (M) and Luke (L). The arguments for Markan priority are these: it explains the pattern of order; Matthew and Luke often smooth Mark's rough Greek; they often soften statements in Mark that might seem to limit Jesus or embarrass the disciples (Mark 6:5 says Jesus could do no miracle in Nazareth, while Matthew 13:58 says he did not do many); and it is easier to see why someone would expand Mark than why someone would abbreviate Matthew and Luke while omitting the birth stories, the Sermon on the Mount, and the resurrection appearances. The case for Q rests mainly on the observation that Luke does not seem to know Matthew's additions to Mark's stories, such as Peter's blessing in Matthew 16:17-19, and places the double tradition sayings in quite different settings. This is the majority view in New Testament scholarship. Its leading modern defenders include John Kloppenborg (The Formation of Q, 1987) and Christopher Tuckett, and the International Q Project published a reconstructed Critical Edition of Q in 2000.

The Farrer Hypothesis (or Farrer-Goulder-Goodacre Hypothesis) accepts that Mark was first but dispenses with Q, holding that Luke used both Mark and Matthew. It was proposed by the Oxford theologian Austin Farrer in an essay titled On Dispensing with Q (1955), developed by Michael Goulder (Luke: A New Paradigm, 1989), and argued most fully by Mark Goodacre (The Case Against Q, 2002). Its defenders point out that Q is a hypothetical document for whose existence there is no direct evidence, and they stress the minor agreements: hundreds of small places where Matthew and Luke agree with each other against Mark in the triple tradition, as in the mockers' question, “Who hit You?”, found in Matthew 26:68 and Luke 22:64 but not in Mark 14:65. On the Two-Source view these agreements must be explained as coincidence, textual corruption, or overlap with Q; on the Farrer view they are what one would expect if Luke knew Matthew. Q's defenders reply that Luke's treatment of Matthew would then be very hard to explain.

The Two-Gospel Hypothesis, also called the Griesbach Hypothesis, rejects Markan priority. It holds that Matthew was written first, that Luke used Matthew, and that Mark wrote last, combining and abbreviating the two. It was proposed by the German scholar Johann Jakob Griesbach in the 1780s, argued most fully in a Latin work of 1789 and 1790, and revived in 1964 by the American scholar William R. Farmer (The Synoptic Problem: A Critical Analysis). Its defenders, including David Dungan, David Peabody, and Allan McNicol (the editor of Beyond the Q Impasse: Luke's Use of Matthew, 1996), point to the testimony of early writers that Matthew was first, to Clement of Alexandria's report (in Eusebius, Church History 6.14) that the Gospels with genealogies were written first, and to places where Mark appears to combine the wording of Matthew and Luke, as in Mark 1:32, “That evening, after sunset”, where Matthew has only the first phrase (“When evening came”, Matthew 8:16) and Luke only the second (“At sunset”, Luke 4:40). The view has a small number of followers today, and critics argue that it cannot explain why Mark would omit so much.

Older and other proposals also have defenders. Augustine, in his Harmony of the Gospels (about 400), held that the Gospels were written in their canonical order, Matthew, Mark, Luke, with Mark following Matthew as an abbreviator; B. C. Butler (The Originality of St Matthew, 1951) and John Wenham (Redating Matthew, Mark and Luke, 1991) argued for forms of this Augustinian view. Robert Lindsey, working in Jerusalem, argued in the 1960s that Luke came first, and more recently Alan Garrow has argued that Matthew was last and used both Mark and Luke.

Finally, some scholars question whether written dependence is the whole story. In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries J. G. Herder and J. K. L. Gieseler proposed that the Gospels drew independently on a fixed oral gospel. Birger Gerhardsson (Memory and Manuscript, 1961) argued that Jesus' disciples memorized his teaching as rabbinic students later memorized their teachers'. Kenneth Bailey, drawing on decades in Middle Eastern village life, described what he called informal controlled oral tradition, in which a community retells its important stories freely but corrects any change to their core (Asia Journal of Theology, 1991), though other scholars, such as Theodore Weeden, have questioned his evidence. James D. G. Dunn (Jesus Remembered, 2003) accepted Markan priority and Q but argued that oral performance explains much of the variation that scholars had treated as editing. Eta Linnemann (Is There a Synoptic Problem?, 1992), a former student of Bultmann who became an evangelical, rejected literary dependence altogether in favor of independent eyewitness testimony. Most scholars now hold that written sources and living oral tradition overlapped for decades, and that any solution must allow for both.

sections.body:
Anyone who reads John after the other three notices the difference at once. John opens not with a genealogy or a birth story but with the Word who was with God in the beginning and who “became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14). Much of the Synoptic material is absent: there are no parables of the kind the Synoptics report, no exorcisms, no account of the transfiguration, and no institution of the Lord's Supper at the Last Supper, where John instead tells of Jesus washing his disciples' feet. Instead John has long discourses and dialogues, with Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, the crowds after the feeding of the five thousand, and the disciples in the upper room (chapters 13 to 17). It has seven ‘I am’ sayings with images, among them “I am the bread of life” (6:35) and “I am the resurrection and the life” (11:25). It calls Jesus' miracles signs and narrates a selection of them. Much of the action is set in Jerusalem and Judea rather than in Galilee, and John mentions three Passovers (2:13; 6:4; 11:55), which is the main reason Christians have long spoken of a three-year ministry. John places the clearing of the temple at the start of Jesus' ministry, and in John the crucifixion takes place on the day of Preparation for the Passover (19:14), while the Synoptics present the Last Supper as a Passover meal.

Early Christians noticed the difference. Clement of Alexandria, as quoted by Eusebius (Church History 6.14.7), said that John, aware that the physical facts had been set out in the other Gospels, wrote a spiritual Gospel. Modern scholars have debated whether John knew the other Gospels. P. Gardner-Smith (Saint John and the Synoptic Gospels, 1938) and C. H. Dodd (Historical Tradition in the Fourth Gospel, 1963) argued that John drew on an independent tradition, sometimes of high historical value; the Leuven scholar Frans Neirynck and others argued that John knew and used Mark or all three Synoptics; Richard Bauckham suggested that John wrote for readers who already knew Mark.

The differences in chronology have several proposed explanations: that John and the Synoptics followed different calendars in use in the first century, that John's ‘Preparation’ refers to the Sabbath of Passover week rather than the day before the meal, or that one writer arranged the chronology for theological reasons (in John, Jesus dies as the Passover lambs are being slaughtered). On the temple clearing, some hold there were two such events; others think John or the Synoptics moved it for thematic reasons. These are real questions, and serious scholars answer them differently.

John also names its source. The Gospel attributes its testimony to ‘the disciple whom Jesus loved’, an unnamed figure at the Last Supper, the cross, and the empty tomb, and says of him, “The one who saw it has testified to this, and his testimony is true.” (19:35; compare 21:24). Tradition identified him with John son of Zebedee. Some scholars, including Bauckham, identify him with a different John, known to Papias as John the Elder, a disciple of Jesus but not one of the Twelve; others think the figure is idealized. The traditions agree that John's Gospel rests on the witness of someone who knew Jesus well.

Since the eighteenth century, scholars have also asked how the Gospels relate to the Jesus of history. The modern quest began with Hermann Samuel Reimarus, whose writings were published after his death by Gotthold Lessing in the 1770s and argued that the disciples had invented the resurrection. D. F. Strauss's Life of Jesus (1835) treated much of the Gospels as myth. Albert Schweitzer's The Quest of the Historical Jesus (German 1906) showed how each nineteenth-century life of Jesus had painted him in its author's own image, and concluded that Jesus was an apocalyptic prophet who expected the end of the world. Bultmann held that little could be known of the historical Jesus beyond the fact of his existence and preaching.

Since the 1980s, the so-called Third Quest has read Jesus firmly within first-century Judaism and has generally been more confident about what can be known. E. P. Sanders (Jesus and Judaism, 1985), John P. Meier (A Marginal Jew, from 1991), and N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996), from different starting points, all hold that a great deal of the Gospel material reflects the historical Jesus. Evangelical scholars such as Craig Blomberg (The Historical Reliability of the Gospels, 1987) have argued for the Gospels' general trustworthiness. Skeptical scholars, such as those of the Jesus Seminar in the 1990s and Bart Ehrman in his popular books, remain doubtful about much of the material, especially the miracles and the claims Jesus makes in John.

The Christian confession is that the Jesus of the Gospels is the real Jesus, crucified under Pontius Pilate and raised bodily on the third day. Paul's summary of the gospel, which he says he received and passed on, already includes that Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Peter and the Twelve (1 Corinthians 15:3-5), and most scholars date that tradition to within a few years of the crucifixion.

Gordon Fee and Douglas Stuart, in their guide How to Read the Bible for All Its Worth, suggest that the Gospels be read in two directions. Reading horizontally means comparing a passage with its parallels in the other Gospels, ideally in a synopsis. The point is not to find contradictions or to flatten the differences, but to notice what each writer chose to include, omit, or change, because that shows his concerns. When Peter confesses Jesus in Mark, he says, “You are the Christ.” (Mark 8:29); in Luke, “The Christ of God.” (Luke 9:20); in Matthew, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” (Matthew 16:16), followed by Jesus' blessing on Peter and the promise to build his church. Each version is true to the event and serves its own Gospel's portrait. Matthew places the great sermon on a mountain (Matthew 5:1), and Luke a similar sermon on “a level place” (Luke 6:17); readers debate whether these are the same occasion told differently or whether Jesus, as a traveling teacher, repeated his teaching in more than one place.

Reading vertically means reading each Gospel as a whole, following its story from beginning to end, noticing its structure, its repeated words and themes, and how each scene builds toward its climax. Most of the misreadings of the Gospels come from reading isolated verses, and many of the apparent problems disappear, or at least become understandable, when a passage is read in the flow of its own book.

Above all, the Gospels are about one person, and they ask the reader the question Jesus asked his disciples: “Who do you say I am?” (Mark 8:29). Mark wrote so that his readers would hear the good news; Luke so that Theophilus might know “the certainty of the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:4); John so that his readers might believe and have life. The four portraits are best read not as rivals but as a chorus.
